title: 📘 UNIT 6: AFRICA AND THE OUTSIDE WORLD 1500–1880s
📌 6.1 CONTACT WITH THE OUTSIDE WORLD
notes:
🇵🇹 Portugal was the first European country to establish early contacts with the coastal regions of West Africa.

🎯 Main objectives of Portuguese exploration:
• Reach India through a new sea route.
• Bypass Muslim North Africa.
• Gain direct access to West African gold.
• Establish commercial links with Africa.
• Spread Christianity.
• Strengthen Christianity against the Ottoman Empire.

💰 African gold was important for financing further Portuguese exploration and trade.

title: 🧭 Prince Henry the Navigator
notes:
Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored Portuguese exploration of Africa.

His major interests included:
• Spreading Christianity.
• Creating commercial links with Africa.
• Using African gold to finance further voyages.
• Opening direct Portuguese access to the Indian Ocean.

title: 🗺️ Early Portuguese Expansion
notes:
📍 1415: Portuguese conquered Ceuta in present-day Morocco.

📍 1432: Reached Cape Bajador.

📍 1441: Nuno Tristão reached Cape Blanc.

📍 1460: Portuguese reached Sierra Leone and became active in Senegambia.

📍 1482: Portuguese built Elmina Castle on the Gold Coast as a permanent trading post.

title: 🏰 Elmina and the Gold Coast
notes:
Elmina Castle was built by the Portuguese in 1482 on the western coast of present-day Ghana.

🎯 Purposes:
• Protect Portuguese trade from European competitors.
• Support trade along the Gold Coast.
• Strengthen Portuguese control of commercial activities.

🌽 European contact also introduced American crops such as maize and cassava, which contributed to population growth in West and Central Africa.

title: 🇪🇺 Other European Powers
notes:
During the 17th and 18th centuries, other European powers joined the competition for overseas trade.

Countries included:
• Netherlands
• England
• France

⚔️ The principal early struggle was between the Dutch and Portuguese.

📍 1642: The Dutch captured Elmina, and the Portuguese left the Gold Coast permanently.

title: 📌 6.2 SLAVERY
notes:
⛓️ Slavery had a long history in Africa, Europe and Asia before the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade.

In the 15th century, enslaved Africans were mainly transported to Southwest Asia, where many were used as domestic servants.

Other historical slave routes included:
• Nubia to Egypt through the Nile.
• Africa across the Sahara to North Africa.
• Northeast Africa to the Persian Gulf and Indian states.

title: ⛓️ Slavery in African Societies
notes:
Slave labour was used in several African societies.

🌾 Mali, Songhai and other states used slave labour in agriculture.

🌾 In Benin, large numbers of slaves were employed in agriculture.

⚠️ Slaves were often treated as private property and were regarded as symbols of wealth and prosperity.

title: 🌊 Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
notes:
The discovery of America in 1492 created conditions for the expansion of the Atlantic slave trade.

🏭 Europeans established plantations and mines in America and needed large numbers of labourers.

Initially, Europeans enslaved Native Americans. Many died from diseases and harsh treatment. Europeans then transported enslaved people from Europe, followed by large-scale transportation of Africans from West Africa.

title: 🔺 Triangular Trade
notes:
The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade was also called the Triangular Trade because it connected three continents:

🌍 Africa
🌎 America
🌍 Europe

AFRICA: Enslaved Africans were exchanged for European goods such as firearms, cotton goods, alcoholic drinks and metal wares.

AMERICA: Enslaved Africans worked on plantations producing sugar, tobacco, coffee and other products.

EUROPE: American raw materials were taken to Europe and manufactured into finished goods.

title: 📊 Three Phases of the Atlantic Slave Trade
notes:
1️⃣ Piratic Slave Trade
15th century to the 1580s.

Individual merchants, adventurers, navigators and sea robbers participated in the trade.

2️⃣ Monopolistic Slave Trade
Began in the 1580s.

Slave-trading companies controlled the trade with official government and military support. The hunting area and volume of trade increased greatly.

3️⃣ Free Trade
Began in the 1690s.

Individual traders increasingly participated, creating strong competition with former monopolistic companies.

title: ⚔️ Circumstances Behind the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade
notes:
Three important circumstances contributed to its development in West Africa:

• Fragmentation of large African political states such as Ghana, Mali and Songhai.

• Growing importance of West Africa as a source of enslaved people.

• Conflicts among small coastal states and their cooperation with European traders in exchanging enslaved people for arms.

title: 📉 Effects of the Slave Trade on Africa
notes:
💰 Economic Effects
• Undermined African craft technology and agriculture.
• Removed labour from agriculture and productive activities.
• Reduced the African working population.
• European nations accumulated enormous wealth.
• European wealth contributed to Western European industrialization.

🏛️ Political Effects
• Increased confusion and insecurity.
• Encouraged violence and warfare.
• Discouraged political development.
• Contributed to the destruction of African states.

title: 👥 Social Effects of the Slave Trade
notes:
• Caused great human suffering and loss of dignity.
• Enslaved people were treated as property rather than human beings.
• Depopulated Africa of many productive young men and women.
• Separated individuals from their families and communities.
• Created long-term social disruption.

📌 The textbook states that historical records indicate more than 12 million Africans were enslaved and deported from Africa.

title: 📌 6.3 THE “LEGITIMATE” TRADE
notes:
🛒 Legitimate trade refers to the trade in commodities between Africans and European merchants after the gradual abolition of the slave trade.

African raw materials, especially cash crops, were exchanged for European manufactured goods.

title: 🌾 Main Commodities in Legitimate Trade
notes:
During the first half of the 19th century, commodities increasingly replaced the export of enslaved people.

Important exports included:
• Palm produce
• Rubber
• Cotton
• Skins
• Cocoa
• Gum Arabic from Senegal
• Groundnuts from Guinea
• Palm oil from coastal forest regions

📈 These products were highly demanded in Europe because of the Industrial Revolution.

title: ⚠️ Effects of Legitimate Trade
notes:
Although the slave trade declined, legitimate trade created new problems.

• Intensified exploitation of African natural resources.
• Increased production of cash crops and raw materials for European industries.
• Did not provide African states with real economic strength and independence.
• Contributed to the expansion of European colonialism.
• Created an unequal trading system.

title: 📌 6.4 WHITE SETTLEMENT IN SOUTH AFRICA
notes:
🇳🇱 In 1652, the Dutch trading company established a small permanent settlement on the southern coast of South Africa.

🎯 Initial purposes:
• Regulate trade with the Khoisan.
• Provide fresh fruit and vegetables for ships.
• Establish a hospital for sick sailors.

This settlement later became the foundation for wider white settlement in South Africa.

title: 👨‍🌾 Boers and the Khoisan
notes:
📍 1657: Van Riebeeck allowed some company soldiers to establish businesses as Boers, meaning farmers.

The Boers were provided with enslaved West Africans.

⚔️ Boer settlement on Khoisan grazing land led to the First Khoi-Dutch War in 1659.

The Khoisan initially united and pushed the Boers back toward the coast.

📍 1673–1677: Second Khoi-Dutch War occurred, after which the Khoisan lost further ground.

title: 🐄 Impact on the Khoisan
notes:
The Dutch expansion caused the Khoisan to lose:

• Material resources.
• Political rights.
• Land and economic independence.
• Parts of their language and cultural identity.

Some Khoisan became herdsmen and hunters for the Boers and adopted aspects of Dutch language and culture.

title: ⚔️ Boers and the Xhosa
notes:
The Trek Boers moved into the fertile grazing lands of Zuurveld.

⚔️ Conflict with the Xhosa began in 1779 and continued for about a century.

The textbook identifies about nine frontier wars during this period.

The Xhosa had a larger population and strong social organization, making them a powerful resistance to colonial expansion.

title: 🇬🇧 British Occupation of the Cape
notes:
📍 1795: Britain seized the Cape Colony from the Dutch for strategic reasons.

Britain wanted to prevent the Cape from falling into French hands.

📍 1818–1819: British forces pushed the Xhosa beyond the Keiskama River.

📍 1829: About 500 British immigrants settled in the newly conquered area.

title: 🚶 Great Trek
notes:
In the 1830s and 1840s, many Dutch-speaking Boers moved northward from the Cape Colony.

Reasons for the Great Trek included:
• Opposition to laws giving freedom to native Africans and coloured people.
• Opposition to ideas of equality between black and white people.
• Dissatisfaction with British policies.
• Opposition to the abolition of slavery.

title: 📌 6.5 EUROPEAN EXPLORERS AND MISSIONARIES
notes:
🧭 Between the 1780s and 1870s, many European explorers travelled into the interior of Africa.

The abolition movement against the slave trade helped stimulate renewed European interest in Africa.

European explorers were motivated by:
• Scientific curiosity.
• Adventure.
• Fame.
• Economic and trading opportunities.
• European colonial expansion.

title: 🧭 Explorers and Colonial Expansion
notes:
Although some explorers presented their journeys as scientific investigations, the people who financed many expeditions were interested in future commercial profits.

📌 European explorers increasingly provided geographical information about Africa and were often direct agents of colonial expansion.

title: ✝️ European Missionaries in Africa
notes:
Roman Catholic missionaries from Portugal followed early Portuguese coastal expansion into tropical Africa.

📍 Late 15th and early 16th centuries:
Catholic missionaries attempted to convert African rulers.

🎯 Their purposes included:
• Spreading Christianity.
• Building alliances with African rulers.
• Supporting Portuguese interests.

title: 🇧🇯 Missionaries in Benin and Kongo
notes:
Missionaries faced resistance when African rulers recognized the political motives behind European religious activities.

🇧🇯 Benin: Portuguese missionaries made little progress. The attempt to convert the Oba was abandoned in the early 16th century.

🇨🇩 Kongo: Missionary activities achieved greater success, and a Christian convert became king in 1506.

title: 🇪🇹 Jesuit Missionaries in Ethiopia
notes:
Portuguese military assistance reached Galadewos in the early 1540s, followed by Jesuit missionaries.

✝️ Their major objective was to convert Ethiopian Orthodox Christians to Roman Catholic Christianity.

❌ They achieved little success.

📍 By the mid-17th century, Jesuit missionaries were expelled because of political interference.

title: ⛪ Protestant Missionaries in the 19th Century
notes:
During the 19th century, European Christian societies increased missionary activities in Africa.

Important missionary organizations included:
• British Anglican Church Missionary Society
• Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society
• London Missionary Society

Protestant missions also came from France, Germany, Holland and the United States.

French Catholic missions followed later in the century.

notes:

⛓️ Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade: Connected Africa, America and Europe.

🔺 Triangular Trade: Africa, America and Europe.

📊 Phases: Piratic → Monopolistic → Free Trade.

🛒 Legitimate Trade: African raw materials exchanged for European goods.

🇿🇦 1652: Dutch permanent settlement established at the Cape.

🚶 Great Trek: Large-scale northward movement of Boers in the 1830s and 1840s.

🧭 European Explorers: Increased European knowledge of Africa and supported commercial and colonial expansion.
